children.translated_text: 1. Chapter on Knowledge //
Having somehow attained the servitude of <s>Maheśvara</s> (the Great Lord),
and wishing to benefit people as well,
I set forth the Recognition of Him,
which is the cause of attaining all prosperity.

children.text: Ipv: parameśvaraprasādād eva labdhātyantadurlabhataddāsyalakṣmīr aham ekākisaṃpadā lajjamāno janam apīmam akhilaṃ svasvāminaṃ vakṣyamāṇopāyena pratyabhijñāpayāmi yena paramārthalābhena parituṣyeyam //
children.translated_text: Vṛtti: I, having obtained by the grace of <s>Parameśvara</s> (the Supreme Lord) alone the extremely rare glory of His servitude, being ashamed of my solitary prosperity, cause all these people to recognize their own master through the means to be explained, so that I may be satisfied by this supreme attainment. //
With regard to <s>Maheśvara</s> (the Great Lord), who is the agent and knower,
one's own Self, established from the beginning,
who, being of non-inert nature, could effect either
a negation or a proof of Him?

children.text: Ipv: sarveṣāṃ svātmanaḥ sarvārthasiddhisamāśrayasya tattatsarvārthasādhanānyathānupapattyā kroḍīkṛtasiddheḥ svaprakāśasya pramātrekavapuṣaḥ pūrvasiddhasya purāṇasya jñānaṃ kriyā ca / svasaṃvedanasiddham aiśvaryaṃ, teneśvarasya siddhau nirākaraṇe ca jaḍānām evodyamaḥ //
children.translated_text: Vṛtti: The knowledge and action of one's own Self—the knower whose identity is the 'I'-consciousness, self-luminous, whose prior establishment is proven by the impossibility of otherwise accomplishing all those various means to all ends, the resort of the accomplishment of all purposes for all beings—these are established through self-awareness as His sovereignty. Therefore, only the inert would exert effort in either establishing or refuting <s>Īśvara</s> (the Lord). //
However, due to the power of delusion, regarding this
which, though seen, is not recognized,
through the manifestation of His powers,
this Recognition is being demonstrated.

children.text: Ipv: kevalam asya svasaṃvedanasiddhasyāpīśvarasya māyāvyāmohād ahṛdayaṃgamatvād asādhāraṇaprabhāvābhijñānakhyāpanena dṛḍhaniścayarūpaṃ pratyabhijñānamātram upadarśyate //
children.translated_text: Vṛtti: Nevertheless, even though this <s>Īśvara</s> is established through self-awareness, due to the bewilderment of <s>Māyā</s>, because it has not been taken to heart, merely the Recognition—in the form of firm certainty—is demonstrated through the declaration of the knowledge of His extraordinary powers. //
For indeed, the foundation of inert entities
rests upon the living;
knowledge and action of entities
are considered the life of the living.

children.text: Ipv: vastūnāṃ jaḍājaḍabhedena dvaividhyam / tatra jaḍasvarūpasya jīvanniṣṭhā siddhiḥ, jīvatāṃ puno jīvatvaṃ jīvanaṃ jñānakriye eva //
children.translated_text: Vṛtti: Things are of two kinds, distinguished as inert and non-inert. Among these, the establishment of the inert nature depends upon the living. But the livingness—the life—of the living is knowledge and action alone. //
Therein, knowledge is self-established;
action, being dependent on the body,
may be observed even by others;
through it, the knowledge of another is inferred.

children.text: Ipv: jīvatāṃ kriyā kāyaparispandaparyantībhūtānyatrāpi pratyakṣā, jñānam ātmavedyaṃ paratrāpi kriyayaiva prasidhyatīti siddha eva svasaṃvedanasaṃvedyatayā svaparayor īśvaro 'haṃpratyeya ātmā, tasya māyāśaktyā nisargatirodhānād evaṃ vimatiḥ //
children.translated_text: Vṛtti: The action of living beings, culminating in bodily movement, is perceptible elsewhere too; knowledge, known to oneself, is established even in others through action alone. Thus the Lord, the Self whose identity is the 'I'-consciousness, knowable through self-awareness in both oneself and others, is already established; due to His natural concealment by the power of <s>Māyā</s>, such doubt arises. //
Thus ends the introduction. //
Thus ends the first lesson in the Chapter on Knowledge. //
Now, knowledge is of one kind, manifesting <s>svalakṣaṇa</s> (the particular),
and another kind,
accompanied by verbal expression, called <s>vikalpa</s> (conceptual thought),
is of many kinds; yet neither is that a duality,
nor does some eternal seer
who does not appear therein—
even this 'I'-awareness
which terminates in the body and such—

children.text: Ipv: jñānam ekaṃ sphuṭāvabhāsasvalakṣaṇānubhavasvarūpaṃ nirvikalpakaṃ te kathayanti / aparaṃ tu śabdāruṣaṇayā smṛtisaṃśayotprekṣādibahubhedaṃ vikalpasaṃjñam / ubhayam apy etan na yujyate bodharūpajñānātiriktasyānyasya saṃbandhitayā tasyānupalabdheḥ / ko 'sau sthirarūpa ātmā ? sābhilāpāhaṃpratyayenāpi śarīrādikavedyavastūttīrṇo vedayitā na kaś cid lokair avadhāryate //
children.translated_text: Vṛtti: They say knowledge of one kind is non-conceptual (<s>nirvikalpaka</s>), whose nature is the experience of clearly manifested particulars. Another kind, through the imposition of words, is called <s>vikalpa</s> (conceptual thought), with many divisions such as memory, doubt, conjecture, and so on. Neither of these two is tenable, since another entity beyond knowledge whose nature is awareness, in the role of the related subject, is not apprehended. Who is that permanent Self? Even by the 'I'-cognition accompanied by verbal expression, no experiencer transcending the body and other knowable objects is ascertained by people. //
Moreover, if at the destruction of an experience
memory follows it,
how could that be? There would be no permanent
Self if it were the experiencer.

children.text: Ipv: smṛtikāle pūrvānubhavanāśāt kathaṃ pūrvārthānubhavāvaṣṭambhadharmā smṛtir jāyeta yadi tadāpi tadanubhavabodho nānuvarteta, yaś cānekakālasthāyī bodhaḥ sa evātmānubhāvitā //
children.translated_text: Vṛtti: At the time of memory, since the previous experience has perished, how could memory—whose nature is to rely on the previous experience of the object—arise, if the awareness of that experience did not also continue at that time? And the awareness that endures across multiple times is itself the Self, the experiencer. //
Even if there is a Self, due to the destruction of perception,
through which could there be memory of the objects perceived through it?
Or else, wherever the experience was,
memory is confined to that very domain.

children.text: Ipv: arthābhāsanāśāt tanmukhāvalambanīyo viṣayo 'py atra nāsti smṛter ity ekabodhātmani saty api ātmani sā nirviṣayaivetivyavahārocchedaḥ / asato 'py arthānubhavasya viṣayeṇa sā viṣayavatī yadi //
children.translated_text: Vṛtti: Since the manifestation of the object has perished, the object too, which depends on that channel, does not exist here for memory. Thus, even when there is a Self whose nature is a single awareness, memory would be without an object—hence the breakdown of practical activity. If memory has an object even when the experience of the object is absent— //
Since memory arises
from the <s>saṃskāra</s> (impression) of a previous experience,
if so, what would be the purpose
of a permanent Self as a superfluous inner element?

children.text: Ipv: anubhavāt saṃskāraḥ saṃskārāc ca smṛtir jāyamānā taṃ pūrvānubhavam anukurvaty evāvagāhitaviṣayaṃ tam anubhavam ābhāsayati / evam ātmasthairyeṇa kim anupayoginā saṃskārasyātmavāde 'py aṅgīkaraṇāt tenaiva ca siddheḥ //
children.translated_text: Vṛtti: Memory, arising from an impression born of experience, reproduces that previous experience and illuminates that experience with its grasped object. What use then is the permanence of the Self, since the <s>saṃskāra</s> (impression) is accepted even in the doctrine of the Self, and everything is accomplished by that alone? //
Therefore, among the mutually distinct <s>dharmas</s> (properties),
given the non-difference of their essential nature,
if memory is established through <s>saṃskāra</s>,
the rememberer would be posited just like the seer.

children.text: Ipv: sukhaduḥkhajñānādibhinnadharmāśrayatvenāpy ātmano 'nupayogo bhinnair dharmair asaṃbhinnasyānupajātaviśeṣasya smṛtav avyāpṛteḥ / tad draṣṭṛvat kalpanāmātram etad ātmā smṛteti //
children.translated_text: Vṛtti: Even as the substrate of distinct properties such as pleasure, pain, knowledge, etc., the Self is useless, since one who is undifferentiated and unmixed with the distinct properties, in whom no distinction has arisen, is not engaged in memory. Therefore, like the seer, this is a mere postulation: 'the Self remembers.' //
If knowledge has the nature of consciousness,
then being impermanent, how could it be like the Self?
Or if it is inert,
how could it have the nature of illuminating objects?

children.text: Ipv: citsvābhāvye jñānasya cety adharmadeśakālāveśayogād ātmana iva nityatādiprasaṅgaḥ / jaḍatve katham arthasyāsau prakāśaḥ //
children.translated_text: Vṛtti: If knowledge has the nature of <s>cit</s> (consciousness), then, due to the impossibility of associating it with different properties, places, and times, there would be the consequence of permanence and so on, just as with the Self. If it were inert, how could it illumine objects? //
Or does the intellect assume the form
of the object, just as it does of the Self?
If its consciousness is non-inert, then in that case,
if inert, it would not illumine objects.

children.text: Ipv: jñānaṃ buddhiḥ / sā jaḍāpi yathā viṣayarūpachāyāṃ dhatte tathātmano 'pi caitanyachāyām, ato 'sav arthaprakāśas tathā ca tasyāś citsvarūpatā syāt / evaṃ jñānaṃ sad api nānyasya saṃbandhi, anupapatteḥ / kriyā tu na svarūpeṇāsti nānyasaṃbandhitayā //
children.translated_text: Vṛtti: Knowledge is the intellect (<s>buddhi</s>). Even though inert, just as it assumes the reflection of the form of the object, so too it assumes the reflection of the consciousness of the Self; hence it illumines objects. In that case, it would have the nature of consciousness. Thus, even existing, knowledge is not related to another entity, since that is untenable. Action, however, does not exist in its own nature, nor through relation to another. //
Action too—the arising of the body and such things
in this or that location—
is not perceived by another; nor is it single,
and the sequential and the unitary are fitting.

children.text: Ipv: kriyāpi pūrvāparībhūtavayavaikā kārakavyāpārarūpā na yuktā kramikasyānekakālaspṛśah svātmāikyāyogāt, nāpi kālakramavyāpī caikasvabhāvaś ca tasyā āśrayo yuktaḥ, kevalaṃ gamanapariṇāmādirūpā sā kriyā / kāyādīnāṃ tu tattadbhinnadeśakālagatapūrvasattāmātram etad atiriktasyānyasyānupalambhāt //
children.translated_text: Vṛtti: Action too, consisting of the operation of instruments, unified though having parts that are prior and posterior, is not tenable for a sequential entity touching multiple times due to the impossibility of unity with its own nature; nor is one of a single nature spanning temporal sequence a fitting substrate for it. That action is merely of the nature of movement, transformation, and so on. For the body and such things, this is merely their prior existence in their respective distinct locations and times, since nothing else beyond that is apprehended. //
That which remains in this or that state
simply becomes this or that—thus it is perceived;
there is no other relation
besides the relation of cause and effect.

children.text: Ipv: pūrvasmin sati parasya sattety etāvanmātre 'nubhavaḥ / kriyāvac ca na kriyākārakasaṃbandhaḥ kaś cid bhinnasyāsyānupalambhāt / kāryakāraṇabhāvād ṛte nānyad vastūnāṃ jñāteyam //
children.translated_text: Vṛtti: Experience amounts to just this much: when the prior exists, the subsequent exists. And there is no relation of action and agent, like that involving action, since this separate entity is not apprehended. Nothing knowable about things exists apart from the causal relation. //
Because a relation, being located in two,
would have multiple forms; because what is already established needs no other;
and because dependence and such cannot apply—
by this reasoning, the agent too is merely posited.

children.text: Ipv: sambandho dviṣṭho na caikenātmanobhayatrāvasthitir yuktā na ca dvayoḥ siddhayor anyonyāpekṣātmā nāpi svātmamātraniṣṭhayoḥ pāratantryarūpaḥ saṃbandhaḥ / tato yathā jñātṛtvaṃ kalpitaṃ tathā kartṛtvam apīti katham ātmā sarveśara iti ? //
children.translated_text: Vṛtti: A relation is located in two terms, yet it is not possible for a single self to be present in both; nor can a relation in the form of mutual dependence exist between two already-established entities; nor can a relation in the form of dependence exist for those resting solely in their own nature. Therefore, just as knowership is posited, so too is agenthood—so how can the Self be the Lord of all? //
True; however, the knowledge that is memory,
though born from the impression of a previous experience,
even though resting in the Self,
does not cognize the original experience.

children.text: Ipv: pūrvānubhavasaṃskāraprabodhajanmāpi smṛtir ātmamātraniṣṭhatvāt svarūpasaṃvedikaiva na tu pūrvānubhavāveśābhāvāt pūrvānubhūtārthavyavasthāpikā ghaṭate //
children.translated_text: Vṛtti: Even memory, whose birth is from the awakening of the impression of a previous experience, because it rests in the Self alone, is merely self-aware and does not succeed in establishing the previously experienced object, due to the absence of being imbued with the previous experience. //
Perception is known only through its own manifestation,
not by another—just as the perception of color is not known by taste;
and the impression-born nature in the case of taste
is mere similarity to it, not reaching it.

children.text: Ipv: sarvā hi jñaptiḥ svasaṃvedanaikarūpānanyasaṃvid dvedhā, rūparasajñānayor anyonyavedane 'nyonyaviṣayavedanam api syāt tataś cendriyaniyamābhāvaḥ / pūrvānubhavasaṃskārajatvena tatsādṛśyamātraṃ na tu pūrvānubhavāvagatiḥ, tatsādṛśyam api nāvaseyam //
children.translated_text: Vṛtti: All cognition, being of the nature of self-awareness alone, a consciousness not of another, is twofold. If there were mutual awareness between the cognitions of color and taste, there would be mutual cognition of each other's objects, and hence there would be no restriction of the sense organs. Through being born from the impression of a previous experience, there is mere similarity to it, not actual cognition of the previous experience; even that similarity is not ascertainable. //
Or, even if memory does not have that as its object,
because it determines that,
its having the seen as its object would be through error—
this is inconsistent.

children.text: Ipv: na cāpi bhrāntyā pūrvānubhavaṃ tadviṣayaṃ ca śuktau rajatam ivāsaṃvedyamānam adhyavasyatīti smṛtis tadviṣayā //
children.translated_text: Vṛtti: Nor does memory, not apprehending the previous experience, determine it and its object through error, like silver in a shell—thus memory would have that as its object. //
How could there be memory from memory alone?
And how could the object's stability depend on error?
And why is dependence on the impression
of a previous experience desired?

children.text: Ipv: pūrvānubhavāprakāśāt tadviṣayasaṃpramoṣe 'dhyavasāyamātrāt smṛtitvaṃ na yuktam / na ca bhrāntyā pūrvānubhūtārthavyavasthāpanam, pūrvānubhavāsparśe ca tadbhinnayogakṣemāyā bhrānteḥ saṃskārajatve ko grahaḥ //
children.translated_text: Vṛtti: Without the illumination of the previous experience, given the loss of its object, memory-hood is not tenable from mere determination alone. Nor does error establish the previously experienced object; and if error, with its own fortune separate from the previous experience, is without contact with it, what is the point of insisting it be impression-born? //
And if the determination is erroneous,
the stability of the object does not come from the inert;
hence, if non-inert, resting in its own impression,
there is no stability of the object from that.

children.text: Ipv: adhyavasāya eva bhrāntyā viṣayavyavasthāpako na tu svasaṃvit, sa ca jaḍaḥ katham arthavyavasthāyā hetuḥ ? cidrūpo 'py atītārthamātram ābhāsayed abāhyasvātmollekhamātraprakāśo vā na taddhetuḥ //
children.translated_text: Vṛtti: Determination alone, through error, establishes the object—not self-awareness. And being inert, how can it be the cause of the object's establishment? Even if of the nature of consciousness, it would illuminate only a past object, or merely illuminate its own inner representation—that cannot be its cause. //
Thus, of cognitions that are mutually distinct
and that do not know each other,
the worldly activity born of their interconnection
would perish, along with people's stability.

children.text: Ipv: jñānāni svātmamātrapariniṣṭhitāni svasaṃvidrūpatayā aparasaṃvedyāni / teṣām anyonyasaṃghaṭṭanāmayaḥ paramārthopadeśaparyanto lokavyavahāraḥ katham //
children.translated_text: Vṛtti: Cognitions, resting solely in their own nature, being of the nature of self-awareness, are unknowable by one another. The worldly activity constituted by their mutual connection, extending to ultimate instruction—how could it exist? //
Unless there be one <s>Maheśvara</s> (Great Lord),
who has internalized the infinite universe as His form,
of the nature of a single consciousness, possessed of the powers
of knowledge, memory, and exclusion.

children.text: Ipv: cittatvam eva viśvarūpamato 'tiriktasyānupapatteḥ, aśeṣapadārthajñānānām anyonyānusaṃdhānam / asyaiva jñānādikāḥ śaktayaḥ / mattaḥ smṛtir jñānam apohanaṃ ceti hy uktam //
children.translated_text: Vṛtti: Consciousness itself is of universal form; therefore, since nothing beyond it is tenable, there is the mutual interconnection of the cognitions of all objects. His alone are the powers of knowledge and so forth. As it is said: 'From Me come memory, knowledge, and their removal.' //
Thus ends the third lesson in the Chapter on Knowledge. //
For He, the object previously experienced,
even when not obtained from another,
reflecting 'that [was I],' at His own will
is said to remember.

children.text: Ipv: paścād api pūrvānubhūtārthānubhavitṛtvāt pūrvānubhūtārthaprakāśāsaṃpramoṣaṇam, tasyaikasya vibhoḥ kartuḥ sa ity atra pūrvānubhūtatvena pratyavamarśaḥ smṛtir nāma vyāparaḥ //
children.translated_text: Vṛtti: Even afterward, because of being the experiencer of the previously experienced object, there is no loss of the illumination of the previously experienced object. For that one Lord, the agent, the reflective awareness 'that [was I]'—recognizing oneself as the one who previously experienced—is the operation called memory. //
And He would illuminate at its own time an object
previously manifested, reflecting upon it—
either through the mere manifestation of the particular
as a pot-appearance, or in its entirety.

children.text: Ipv: smṛtiśaktyā sa iti pūrvānubhūtaṃ svalakṣaṇaṃ parāmṛśann ābhāsayaty evānyathā prakāśitasya parāmarśo na kṛtaḥ syāt svasattākāla eva ca, tena smaraṇakāle naṣṭasyāpy ābhāso na duṣyati / kadā cit tv arthitāvaśād ghaṭakāñcanadravyasattādyanyatamaikābhāsarūpeṇaivāsya sphuṭāvabhāsaḥ, anyadā tu sarvātmanārthitvena tathaiva / atiśayanirantarāvahitacetasas tu dṛṣṭārthapratyakṣīkāra eva //
children.translated_text: Vṛtti: Through the power of memory, reflecting upon the previously experienced particular as 'that,' He illuminates it—for otherwise no reflective awareness of the manifested would have been made—and at the very time of its existence. Therefore, the manifestation of what has perished at the time of recollection is not faulty. Sometimes, due to the force of need, His clear manifestation takes the form of one of the aspects—such as a pot, gold, or the substance's existence; at other times, entirely, due to full interest. But for one whose attention is exceedingly focused and unbroken, there is the very direct perception of the seen object. //
And it would not be proper, if memory were different,
for the remembered object to appear;
hence this unity of cognitions across different times
is known—He is that [same Self].

children.text: Ipv: pūrvānubhūtaś cārtho 'nubhavena saha tātkālikasmṛtiprakāśe 'vabhāsamānaḥ smṛtyabhinna eva prakāśād bhinnasya prakāśamānatānupapatteḥ / evaṃ cānubhavasmṛtyādisaṃvidām aikyaṃ sa eva cātmā vedakaḥ / tathā hi //
children.translated_text: Vṛtti: And the previously experienced object, appearing in the simultaneous illumination of memory along with the experience, is indeed non-different from memory, since what is different from illumination cannot be the subject of illumination. Thus there is the unity of cognitions such as experience and memory, and He alone is the Self, the knower. For indeed: //
For the previous experience does not appear
in memory as separate, like its object;
because of the manifestation as 'I previously experienced'—
the Self ascending into awareness.

children.text: Ipv: smṛtau smaryamāṇo 'nubhūtārtho yathā pṛthagbhūto bhāti na tathānubhavaḥ svātmana evāhaṃtāpratyeyasyānubhavamayatvena prathanāt, yaś cānekakālo 'haṃvedyo 'rthaḥ sa evātmā //
children.translated_text: Vṛtti: In memory, the remembered previously-experienced object appears as separate, but not so the experience—because of its manifestation as being of the nature of the 'I'-consciousness, which is the Self's own experience. And the entity known as 'I' across multiple times is the Self itself. //
Even for <s>yogins</s>, perceptions do not appear
within another's perception;
being of the measure of their own self-awareness alone,
they would appear even in the domain of the knowable.

children.text: Ipv: sarvajñānām api pramātrāntaragatopalambhāḥ svasaṃvinmātravedyasvabhāvāḥ svātmārūḍhā eva bhāseran, ataś ca teṣāṃ yogināṃ parātmatāpattir eva tattvam / prameyakakṣyāyām api ghaṭādivat prātisvikena śuddhabodhātmanā rūpeṇāvabhāseran yadi tathā saṃbhavet /
children.translated_text: Vṛtti: Even for the omniscient, perceptions present in another knower, being of the nature of what is knowable only through self-awareness, would appear only as mounted upon their own Self. Hence, for those <s>yogins</s>, the truth is indeed the identity with other selves. They would appear in the domain of the knowable too, in the form of their own nature which is pure awareness, like a pot and so on, if that were possible. //
What is remembered: 'there was a perception of mine'—
this too, from the standpoint of difference,
is the analysis of this very memory
'I perceived'—that is all.

children.text: Ipv: mayā dṛṣṭam iti pramātrāntargatadarśanaparāmarśātmikāyā eva smṛter vibhajya kathanam, etad evam anubhavo 'sau mamābhūd iti bhedenāpi nirdeśaḥ /
children.translated_text: Vṛtti: 'I perceived'—of this very memory, whose nature is the reflective awareness of the perception contained within the knower, the separate narration—'that experience of mine was such'—is also an expression through differentiation. //
And that cognition 'I see this,'
or 'this is a pot'—the determination—
also considers perception as
conjoined with the determiner.

children.text: Ipv: paraḥsthitārthavikalpane 'pi ghaṭam imaṃ paśyāmi ghaṭo 'yam iti vā pramātṛmayam eva darśanaṃ pratyavamṛśyate //
children.translated_text: Vṛtti: Even in the conceptual cognition of an object present before one, 'I see this pot' or 'this is a pot'—perception is reflectively cognized as being of the nature of the knower. //
Thus: 'this is perceived by me,'
'this is he who was seen'—reflecting upon both,
the objects of grasped and grasper, as non-different,
have appeared in the knower.

children.text: Ipv: tasmād dṛkparāmarśapuraḥsārāyāṃ smṛtau vikalpamātre vā dṛkṣabdānuvedhaṃ vināpi sa ity ayam iti vārthamātranirdeśena sarvatraikapramātṛlīnav evānubhāvyānubhāvakau māyākṛtavicchinnāvabhāsav api prakāśete //
children.translated_text: Ipv: Therefore, in memory which is preceded by the apprehension of perception, or in mere <s>vikalpa</s> (conceptual construction), even without the pervasion of the word 'perception' (<s>dṛk</s>), by merely indicating the object as 'he' or 'this,' the experienced and the experiencer, though their manifestations are severed by <s>Māyā</s>, shine forth as always merged in a single knowing subject (<s>ekapramātṛ</s>).
Thus ends the fourth <s>āhnika</s> (chapter) in the <s>Jñānādhikāra</s> (Section on Knowledge).
Of presently manifest
entities, the manifestation
is possible only of those abiding within,
externally, by the Self.

children.text: Ipv: pratyakṣe 'pi yāvad arthānāṃ bhedenāvabhāsaḥ pramātrantarlīnānām eva satāṃ yuktaḥ //
children.translated_text: Ipv: Even in direct perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>), the manifestation of objects as distinct is proper only when they exist as merged within the knowing subject (<s>pramātṛ</s>).
As before, an object would be unmanifest
without having the nature of <s>prakāśa</s> (light/consciousness),
and <s>prakāśa</s> cannot be separate —
the very nature of the object is its luminosity (<s>prakāśatā</s>).

children.text: Ipv: pramātṛsaṃjñaprakāśasvarūpatāṃ vinā yathādau ghaṭo 'sya nāvabhāsas tathā jñānakāle 'pi syāt, prakāśamānatā cārthasya prakāśaḥ svarūpato na tu bhinnaḥ //
children.translated_text: Ipv: Without having the nature of <s>prakāśa</s> (light/consciousness), designated as the knowing subject (<s>pramātṛ</s>), just as a pot was not manifest to him at first, so too it would remain even at the time of cognition; and the being-manifest of an object is <s>prakāśa</s> (consciousness) in its essential nature, not something separate.
If <s>prakāśa</s> were separate, or even if unseparate,
there would be confusion of objects; therefore
the object to be illumined has <s>prakāśa</s> as its nature —
and an unmanifest object cannot be established.

children.text: Ipv: prakāśamātraṃ cārthād bhinnaṃ sarvārthasādhāraṇaṃ tasya ghaṭasya prakāśo 'yam ayaṃ paṭasyaiveti viṣayaniyamo nirnibandhanaḥ / tasmād arthasya siddhiḥ prakāśātmatāyattā //
children.translated_text: Ipv: If <s>prakāśa</s> (illumination) alone, separate from the object, were common to all objects, then the determination of the object — 'this is the illumination of that pot, this belongs to the cloth alone' — would be without basis. Therefore, the establishment of an object depends on its having <s>prakāśa</s> as its nature.
If each spontaneous manifestation
were to indicate something external,
then undifferentiated cognition (<s>bodha</s>) could not
be the cause of varied manifestations.

children.text: Ipv: jaḍānām ābhāsamānataiva sattāsiddhiḥ sā ca ābhāsātmataiva / tataś ca bodhamātram ekam evātra tattvam / tasyāviśeṣe 'pi krameṇa viśiṣyamāṇo 'rthāvabhāsas tato 'nyam aprakāśamānaṃ hetutayā bāhyam artham ūhayed indiyavat //
children.translated_text: Ipv: For inert things, their very state of being manifest is the proof of their existence, and that is nothing but having manifestation (<s>ābhāsa</s>) as their nature. Therefore, <s>bodha</s> (cognition/awareness) alone is the single reality here. Even though it is without differentiation, when the manifestation of objects becomes progressively differentiated, one might infer from that an external object, not itself manifest, as a cause — like the sense organs.
Nor could the awakening of <s>vāsanās</s> (latent impressions)
in their variety serve as the cause here,
for that very awakening too —
what is the basis for its variety?

children.text: Ipv: vicitravāsanāprabodho na bodhād bhinnaḥ, tasyāpi vaicitrye ko hetuḥ / tato bāhya evārtho bhinnābhāsahetuḥ //
children.translated_text: Ipv: The varied awakening of <s>vāsanās</s> (latent impressions) is not different from cognition (<s>bodha</s>); for the variety of that awakening too, what is the cause? Therefore, it is only an external object that is the cause of differentiated manifestation.
One might say: since with respect to those manifestations
themselves the matter is settled,
what need is there of another
external thing, which is logically untenable?

children.text: Ipv: ābhāsamānair eva arthair vyavahāraḥ, te cābhāsātmakāḥ santu kā kṣatiḥ / tat kiṃ bāhyena kāryaṃ tāvatā lokayātrāsamāpteḥ / bāhyaś cārthaḥ pramāṇabādhitaḥ sāvayavo viruddhadharmādhyāsāder niravayavaś ca dikṣaṭkayogāder bahuśaḥ //
children.translated_text: Ipv: Practical activity (<s>vyavahāra</s>) proceeds with objects as they are manifest, and let them have <s>ābhāsa</s> (manifestation) as their nature — what harm is there? What need then for an external object, since worldly affairs are accomplished by that much alone? Moreover, the external object is refuted by valid means of knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>) — if it has parts, due to the superimposition of contradictory properties, and if partless, due to problems like contact with the six directions, and so on, in many ways.
The Lord, whose nature is <s>Cit</s> (consciousness), dwelling within,
by the power of will (<s>icchā</s>), externally,
like a <s>yogī</s>, without any material cause (<s>upādāna</s>),
would manifest the entire world of objects.

children.text: Ipv: cittattvam eva īśvaratvāt svātmarūpatayā upapannābhāsanam anantaśaktitvād icchāvaśān mṛdādikāraṇaṃ vinaiva bāhyatvena ghaṭapaṭādikam artharāśiṃ prakāśayet //
children.translated_text: Ipv: The <s>Cit</s>-principle (consciousness-reality) itself, being the Lord (<s>Īśvara</s>), manifesting as its own nature, possessing infinite powers (<s>anantaśakti</s>), by the power of will (<s>icchā</s>), without any material cause such as clay, would manifest externally the entire mass of objects such as pots, cloths, and so forth.
Inference — regarding what was not previously manifest —
is not at all accepted; the sense organ
is itself manifest; from the manifestation of seeds and such
the causal entity is established from manifestation alone.

children.text: Ipv: pūrvāvabhātāntaḥsthita evārthe nāntarīyakārthadarśanavaśāt tattaddeśakālādiyojanayā vimarśanam anumānam / indriyam apy anumīyate kiṃcinmātraṃ nimittaṃ tac ca bījādyābhāsād ābhāsitam eva //
children.translated_text: Ipv: Inference (<s>anumāna</s>) is the reflective cognition (<s>vimarśana</s>) regarding an object that abides within, having been previously manifest, through the force of perceiving a necessary concomitant, by connecting it with particular place, time, and so forth. The sense organ too is inferred as merely some kind of cause, and that is established as manifest from the manifestation of seeds and the like.
The manifestation of an external thing
could never arise from manifestation;
therefore neither is the object established,
nor can it be established through inference.

children.text: Ipv: ghaṭādyābhāsād bāhyasyānupapatter nāsīd ābhāsaḥ, tatas tatra nānumānād api siddhiḥ //
children.translated_text: Ipv: Because an external thing cannot be established from the manifestation of pots and such, it has no manifestation; therefore regarding that, there is no establishment even through inference.
And the manifestation of the entire realm of entities
abiding within the Self
of the sovereign — this certainly exists; without that,
the reflective awareness (<s>vimarśa</s>) in the form of will (<s>icchā</s>) would not operate.

children.text: Ipv: cidātmanaś ceśvarasya ātmanīvābhedenārtheṣv api prakāśe 'sty anyathā pratibhāsamānārthaikaviṣayo nirmātṛtāmayo vimarśa icchārūpo na syāt //
children.translated_text: Ipv: For the Lord (<s>Īśvara</s>) whose nature is <s>Cit</s> (consciousness), when objects too are illumined in non-difference, as if within the Self — otherwise the reflective awareness (<s>vimarśa</s>) in the form of will (<s>icchā</s>), having as its single object the objects that appear as if reflected, consisting in creatorship (<s>nirmātṛtā</s>), would not arise.
They know <s>vimarśa</s> (reflective awareness) to be the essential nature
of manifestation; otherwise,
<s>prakāśa</s> (consciousness), though colored by objects,
would be inert like crystal and such.

children.text: Ipv: prakāśasya mukhya ātmā pratyavamarśaḥ, taṃ vinā arthabheditākārasyāpy asya svacchatāmātraṃ na tv ajāḍyaṃ camatkṛter abhāvāt //
children.translated_text: Ipv: The principal self of <s>prakāśa</s> (light/consciousness) is <s>pratyavamarśa</s> (reflective self-awareness); without it, even though <s>prakāśa</s> has the form of being differentiated by objects, there would be mere transparency but not non-inertness, due to the absence of the wonder of recognition (<s>camatkṛti</s>).
From the Self itself arises <s>caitanya</s> (sentience),
<s>citkriyā</s> (the activity of consciousness), the agency of <s>Citi</s> (consciousness) —
this has been stated with emphasis; by that
it is distinguished from the inert.

children.text: Ipv: ātmadravyasya bhāvātmakam apy etaj jaḍād bhedakatayā vimarśākhyaṃ mukhyaṃ rūpam uktaṃ caitanyaṃ dṛśiśaktiś citir iti [adopt var: citiśaktir dṛśir iti] / sā cetanakriyā citikartṛtaiva //
children.translated_text: Ipv: Of the substance that is the Self, though it has the nature of existence, this principal form called <s>vimarśa</s> (reflective awareness), which differentiates it from the inert, has been stated as <s>caitanya</s> (sentience), the power of seeing (<s>dṛśiśakti</s>), <s>Citi</s> (consciousness). And that conscious activity is nothing but the agency of <s>Citi</s>.
<s>Citi</s> (consciousness), whose nature is <s>pratyavamarśa</s> (reflective self-awareness),
is the supreme Speech (<s>Parā Vāk</s>), arisen from its own essence;
this is the principal <s>svātantrya</s> (absolute freedom),
that is the <s>aiśvarya</s> (sovereignty) of the Supreme Self.

children.text: Ipv: abhinnavācyādyā vāg eṣā nityacitsvarūpatvenānādyantāparatantrā, bhāvāntarānapekṣaṃ śuddham etat svātantryam aiśvaryasaṃjñam //
children.translated_text: Ipv: This Speech (<s>Vāk</s>), in which the signified and so forth are undifferentiated, being eternally of the nature of <s>Cit</s> (consciousness), is without beginning or end and not dependent on anything else. This is the pure <s>svātantrya</s> (absolute freedom), designated as <s>aiśvarya</s> (sovereignty).
That is <s>sphurattā</s> (vibrant luminosity), the great Existence (<s>mahāsattā</s>),
not delimited by space or time;
this itself has been declared as the essence,
the Heart (<s>hṛdaya</s>) of the Supreme Lord.

children.text: Ipv: sphuradrūpatā sphuraṇakartṛtā abhāvāpratiyoginy abhāvavyāpinī sattā bhavattā bhavanakartṛtā nityā deśakālāsparśāt saiva pratyavamarśātmā citikriyāśāktiḥ / sā viśvātmanaḥ parameśvarasya svātmapratiṣṭhārūpā hṛdayam iti tatra tatrāgame nigadyate //
children.translated_text: Ipv: The nature of being vibrant (<s>sphuradrūpatā</s>), the agency of flashing forth (<s>sphuraṇakartṛtā</s>), is Existence (<s>sattā</s>) — that which has no counter-positive in non-existence, that which pervades even non-existence — Being (<s>bhavattā</s>), the agency of becoming (<s>bhavanakartṛtā</s>), eternal because untouched by space and time. That very power of the activity of <s>Citi</s> (consciousness), whose nature is <s>pratyavamarśa</s> (reflective self-awareness) — it is called in various <s>Āgamas</s> (scriptures) the Heart (<s>hṛdaya</s>), the form of self-establishment of the Supreme Lord whose nature is the universe.
For this very reason, He would make
the Self itself an object of knowledge, as if standing apart;
but the knowable would not — by its orientation toward that —
diminish His <s>svatantratā</s> (absolute freedom).

children.text: Ipv: etādṛśaśuddhasvātantryavaśān naiṣa pṛthag eva labdhapratiṣṭhaṃ vastv avaiti, api tv ajñeyam ātmānam aniyantritaprabhāvatayā jñeyīkaroti / bhinnajñeyasāpekṣatve jñānakartṛtā mlāyet //
children.translated_text: Ipv: By virtue of such pure <s>svātantrya</s> (absolute freedom), He does not cognize a thing that has gained independent standing separately; rather, He makes the Self — which is not an object of knowledge — into an object of knowledge, through His unrestricted power. If the agency of knowing depended on a separate knowable, it would wither.
The Lord, whose Self is not released from <s>svātantrya</s> (freedom),
by <s>svātantrya</s> of His non-dual nature,
through conceptual constructions such as 'the Lord' (<s>Īśa</s>) and so forth,
having created, would engage in practical activity.

children.text: Ipv: ata eva vedyaikībhāvalakṣaṇapūrṇatāmayāt svātantryāt tadānīntanam eva vedakam ātmānam īśvaraḥ śivo veditety evamādivikalpair ābhāsayati bhāvanādivyavahārārtham //
children.translated_text: Ipv: For this very reason, from <s>svātantrya</s> (freedom) which consists in the fullness characterized by unity with the knowable, <s>Īśvara</s> (the Lord) manifests the very knower (<s>vedaka</s>) of that time as the Self, through <s>vikalpas</s> (conceptual constructions) such as 'the Lord,' '<s>Śiva</s>,' 'the knower,' and so on — for the purpose of practical activity such as meditation (<s>bhāvanā</s>).
There is no objectivity (<s>idantā</s>) in the reflective awareness (<s>parāmarśa</s>) of 'I' and so forth
through difference, for this one whose nature is otherwise;
rather, by being the content of the 'I'-reflective awareness itself,
His creation is like the object denoted by verbal endings (<s>tiṅ</s>).

children.text: Ipv: vartamānapramātṛbhāve nāhaṃpratyavamarśasya prameyatvenedantā / vimarśabhede cābhāsabhede ca pramātaiveśvaraśabdena sṛṣṭo 'haṃ parāmarśavyavadhānena kevalam, yathā kriyādiśabdena pacatyādivācyo 'rthaḥ / yathāhuḥ kriyāguṇajātisaṃbandhādiśābdair na kriyādaya ucyante pacatyādimukhenābhidhānāt / īśvaraśabdād ātmaśabdāc cāham iti parāmṛśan na evātmānam avaiti na sākṣāt, pratītis tv asty eva smṛtyevānubhavamukhenānubhūtasya //
children.translated_text: Ipv: In the state of the present knowing subject (<s>pramātṛ</s>), the 'I'-reflective self-awareness (<s>ahaṃpratyavamarśa</s>) does not have the nature of objecthood (<s>idantā</s>) as a knowable. And when there is differentiation in <s>vimarśa</s> (reflective awareness) and differentiation in <s>ābhāsa</s> (manifestation), the knowing subject himself is created by the word '<s>Īśvara</s>' through the mediation of the 'I'-reflective awareness — just as the meaning expressed by words like 'cooks' is expressed through action-words and such. As they say: through words denoting action, quality, universal, relation, and so forth, it is not actions etc. that are directly denoted, but rather they are expressed through forms like 'cooks' and so on. One who reflects 'I' through the word '<s>Īśvara</s>' or the word 'Self' (<s>ātma</s>) does not cognize the Self directly — not face to face; but the cognition certainly exists, through the medium of experience, as in memory of what was previously experienced.
By the <s>Māyā</s>-power of the all-pervading Lord, that very same [consciousness],
having differentiated knowables as its domain,
is called by the names: cognition (<s>jñāna</s>), intention (<s>saṃkalpa</s>),
determination (<s>adhyavasāya</s>), and so forth.

children.text: Ipv: prakāśātmanaḥ parameśvarasya māyāśaktyā svātmarūpaṃ viśvaṃ bhede ābhāsyate / tataḥ saiva citir jñānam adhyakṣam / tasyaiva bhinnasyābhātasya smṛtiḥ saṃkalpo 'dhyavasāyo manobuddhirūpatve 'pi citir eva //
children.translated_text: Ipv: Of the Supreme Lord whose nature is <s>prakāśa</s> (light/consciousness), by <s>Māyā</s>-power the universe, which is His own nature, is manifested in differentiation. Then that very <s>Citi</s> (consciousness) is cognition (<s>jñāna</s>), direct perception (<s>adhyakṣa</s>). Of that very differentiated manifest [content], memory (<s>smṛti</s>), intention (<s>saṃkalpa</s>), determination (<s>adhyavasāya</s>) — though having the form of mind (<s>manas</s>) and intellect (<s>buddhi</s>), it is <s>Citi</s> alone.
Even at the moment of direct perception (<s>sākṣātkāra</s>)
<s>vimarśa</s> (reflective awareness) exists; how otherwise
could activities like running and such
take place without recognition (<s>pratisaṃdhāna</s>)?

children.text: Ipv: sākṣātkāralakṣaṇe jñāne 'pi cito 'rthapratyavamarśo 'sti sūkṣmaḥ, vācanadhāvanādau śīghrakriyā tattaddṛśyamānadeśādyupāditsājihāsānusaṃdhānena hi bhavet //
children.translated_text: Ipv: Even in cognition characterized as direct perception (<s>sākṣātkāra</s>), there is a subtle reflective awareness (<s>pratyavamarśa</s>) of the object by <s>Citi</s> (consciousness); for rapid actions such as reading and running would occur through the connecting recognition of the desire to obtain or avoid the various places and so forth that are being perceived.
'This is a pot' — this determination (<s>adhyavasāya</s>)
transcends name and form;
it is the power of the Supreme Lord, shining
as if the Self, not as objectivity (<s>idantā</s>).

children.text: Ipv: ayam iti ghaṭa iti vādhyavasāyo bhinnaprakāśamānanāmarūpātiriktaś citiśaktimaya evātmevābhedena avabhāsate //
children.translated_text: Ipv: The determination 'this' or 'a pot' — transcending the name and form that are manifest as differentiated — consists of the power of <s>Citi</s> (consciousness) alone and shines in non-difference, as if the Self.
Only because of the conformity
to differentiated objects in particular places and times,
cognition, memory, determination, and so forth
appear in sequence.

children.text: Ipv: cittattvasya māyāśaktyā bhinnaṃ ghaṭādi saṃvedyaṃ tattaddeśakālabhinnaṃ prakāśyate yasyābhedenāvaṣṭambhād vibhinnadeśakālādinā jñānasmṛtyādyābhāsate //
children.translated_text: Ipv: By the <s>Māyā</s>-power of the <s>Cit</s>-principle (consciousness-reality), differentiated objects such as pots are illuminated as distinct in their respective places and times; because of the grasping of these in non-difference, cognition, memory, and so forth manifest as having different places, times, and so on.
Thus ends the fifth <s>āhnika</s> (chapter) in the <s>Jñānādhikāra</s> (Section on Knowledge).
The 'I'-reflective self-awareness (<s>ahaṃpratyavamarśa</s>),
though having <s>prakāśa</s> as its nature, is the body of Speech (<s>Vāk</s>);
it is not <s>vikalpa</s> (conceptual construction), for that has been defined
as a determination that involves a duality.

children.text: Ipv: prakāśasyātmany ahamiti parāvāgrūpatvāt sābhilāpo 'pi svabhāvabhūtaḥ pratyavamarśo na vikalpa ity ucyate, sa hi pratiyoginiṣedhapūrvo niścayo na cātra pratiyogisaṃbhavaḥ //
children.translated_text: Ipv: The <s>pratyavamarśa</s> (reflective self-awareness) 'I' with respect to <s>prakāśa</s> (consciousness) itself, though involving verbal expression due to its being the form of <s>Parā Vāk</s> (Supreme Speech), is its essential nature and is not called <s>vikalpa</s> (conceptual construction); for <s>vikalpa</s> is a determination preceded by the negation of a counter-positive, and here there is no possibility of a counter-positive.
For the manifestation of two distinct things
such as pot and non-pot would require duality;
but of <s>prakāśa</s> alone, there is no
manifestation of another that is different.

children.text: Ipv: prakāśād dvitīyasya bhinnasya pratiyogino 'prakāśasaṃjñasyānavabhāsane prakāśetaratvaṃ na syāt / tasyānābhāse vyapohanāyogād vikalpatāhāniḥ //
children.translated_text: Ipv: Without the manifestation of a second, different counter-positive called 'non-<s>prakāśa</s>' from <s>prakāśa</s>, the otherness of <s>prakāśa</s> would not exist. In the absence of its manifestation, since exclusion (<s>vyapohana</s>) is impossible, the status of being a <s>vikalpa</s> is lost.
Moreover,
by the sheer exclusion of what is 'not-that'
from what partakes of the appearance of 'that and not-that,'
the <s>vikalpa</s> (conceptual construction) 'this is a pot'
is precisely a determination of that.

children.text: Ipv: pramātur eva svatantrasyāntarlīnatadatadarthābhāsasya atadapohanena ghaṭa iti niścayo vikalpo nāma vyāpāraḥ //
children.translated_text: Ipv: It is of the autonomous knowing subject (<s>pramātṛ</s>) alone, within whom the manifestations of 'that' and 'not-that' objects are merged, that the determination 'pot' through the exclusion of 'not-that' constitutes the operation called <s>vikalpa</s>.
When, by <s>Māyā</s>, abandoning the <s>Cit</s>-principle (consciousness-reality),
one who manifests as differentiated —
whether in the body, in the intellect (<s>buddhi</s>), or in the vital breath (<s>prāṇa</s>),
or in the conceived void like space,
the reflective awareness 'I' as a knowing subject,
being an exclusion of the other,
is <s>vikalpa</s> (conceptual construction) alone — that other
counter-positive arises from manifestation.

children.text: Ipv: cidacittattvasyaiveśvarasya māyāśaktyā bhedāvabhāsini śarīre buddhav āntare vā sparśe taduttīrṇe vākāśa iva śūnya eva vikalpite 'hamiti pramātṛbhāvena vimarśaḥ, tattadābhāsamānaśarīrādipratiyogyapohanakaraṇād ghaṭo 'yam itivad vikalpa eva //
children.translated_text: Ipv: When <s>Īśvara</s> (the Lord) himself, whose nature is both <s>Cit</s> and <s>Acit</s> (consciousness and non-consciousness), by <s>Māyā</s>-power manifests differentiation in the body, in the internal intellect (<s>buddhi</s>), or in touch, or in something transcending that, conceived as void like space — the reflective awareness 'I' as a knowing subject (<s>pramātṛ</s>), because it involves the exclusion of the counter-positive of the respectively manifesting body and so forth, is <s>vikalpa</s> (conceptual construction) alone, just like 'this is a pot.'
The connecting of previous manifestation and so forth
with an occasional manifestation
is called conceptualization (<s>kalpanā</s>) based on <s>saṃskāra</s> (latent impression) —
that too operates in differentiated manifestation.

children.text: Ipv: vichinnavicchinneṣu śūnyadehādyābhāsabhedeṣu pūrvābhāsāhaṃkārākhyānām aikyayojanāntaḥpūrvābhāsasthitilakṣaṇasaṃskārāśritā pramātṛvyāpārarūpā kalpanaiva pratyabhijñākhyā //
children.translated_text: Ipv: In the discontinuous, interrupted differences of manifestation such as void, body, and so forth, the conceptualization called recognition (<s>pratyabhijñā</s>), which consists in the connecting into unity of the previous manifestations and the 'I'-sense, depending on the <s>saṃskāra</s> (latent impression) characterized by the persistence of previous manifestation within — is indeed an operation of the knowing subject in the realm of differentiated manifestation.
Thus, even in worldly activity,
the Lord, entering the body and such,
the mass of objects shining within alone,
by will (<s>icchā</s>), manifests externally.

children.text: Ipv: ādisarge vā vyavahāre 'pi vā maheśvaro māyāśaktyā dehādim ātmatvena abhiniviśya pramātāraṃ kurvann antaḥsthitaṃ vibhāntam eva taṃ tam arthaṃ krameṇa bahīrūpaṃ kartṛśaktyā bhāsayati / tathābhāsanam evotpādanam / asya dehādyanāviṣṭasya tu svato yugapad ahamidam iti sarvārthaprakāśaḥ //
children.translated_text: Ipv: Whether in the initial creation or in worldly activity, <s>Maheśvara</s> (the Great Lord), by <s>Māyā</s>-power, entering the body and such and making them the Self, constituting the knowing subject, manifests that very mass of objects abiding within, already shining, progressively as external through the power of agency (<s>kartṛśakti</s>). Such manifestation is itself production. But for Him who has not entered body and such, there is spontaneously the simultaneous illumination of all objects as 'I-this' (<s>aham-idam</s>).
Thus, in memory or even in <s>vikalpa</s> (conceptual construction)
which is devoted to exclusion (<s>apohana</s>),
or even in cognition, the inner manifestation
is ever established — this is certain.

children.text: Ipv: sarvasaṃvitsu sarvārthāvabhāsaḥ pramātṛsaṃlīnaś cittattvavad ānurūpyeṇa prakāśamānaḥ sadā sthita eva //
children.translated_text: Ipv: In all forms of awareness (<s>saṃvit</s>), the manifestation of all objects, merged in the knowing subject, shining in conformity with the <s>Cit</s>-principle, is always ever established.
However, in cognition, which has the nature of
external manifestation, it is innate;
but in memory and such, it persists
in the form of previous experience.

children.text: Ipv: jñāne bahirābhāsanarūpe sahaja eva cittattvasyāntararthāvabhāsaḥ, smṛtyādau tu pūrvānubhavātmā / ata eva smṛtiḥ saṃskārajocyate //
children.translated_text: Ipv: In cognition, which has the form of external manifestation, the inner manifestation of objects belonging to the <s>Cit</s>-principle is innate (<s>sahaja</s>). But in memory and such, it has the nature of previous experience. For this very reason, memory is said to be born of <s>saṃskāra</s> (latent impression).
That [inner manifestation] is innate
even in freely-operating <s>vikalpa</s> (conceptual construction);
because it manifests configurations
as desired, in the domain of the intellect (<s>buddhi</s>).

children.text: Ipv: avatantras tu vikalpaś cakṣurādyagocaram api buddhaviṣayatāpādanena yathāruci pūrvānubhūtatvāvimarśanena navam eva taṃ tam artham ābhāsayati saṃniveśaviśeṣaṃ ca / tatrāsav arthaḥ sahaja evāsti //
children.translated_text: Ipv: Free-ranging <s>vikalpa</s> (conceptual construction), even with respect to what is beyond the range of the eyes and other senses, by bringing it into the domain of <s>buddhi</s> (intellect), manifests at will each object and its particular arrangement as if entirely new, without reflecting on its having been previously experienced. In that, this object-content exists innately.
For this very reason, from the manifestation of
delineation as desired,
the two [powers] of knowledge and action are clearly
established for every living being.

children.text: Ipv: apūrvārthanirmāṇajñānasāmārthyāc ca vikalpa eva sarvasya sarvajñatvaṃ sarvakartṛtvaṃ ca sphuṭam
children.translated_text: Ipv: And because of the capacity of <s>vikalpa</s> (conceptual construction) to create novel objects, omniscience (<s>sarvajñatva</s>) and omnipotence (<s>sarvakartṛtva</s>) are clearly [established] for everyone.
Thus ends the sixth <s>āhnika</s> (chapter) in the <s>Jñānādhikāra</s> (Section on Knowledge).
Seventh <s>āhnika</s> (chapter).
That <s>pratibhā</s> (intuitive flash) which
is adorned by the sequence of various objects —
the knowing subject (<s>pramātṛ</s>) is of the nature of non-sequential, infinite consciousness (<s>Cit</s>);
He is <s>Maheśvara</s> (the Great Lord).

children.text: Ipv: tattatpadārthakramācchuritaś caiṣo 'ntaḥsthita eva ābhāsaḥ sarvasaṃvitkālavyāpyakramānantacinmaya ātmasaṃjñaḥ pramātā svāṅgabhūte prameye nirmātṛtayā maheśvaraś ca //
children.translated_text: Ipv: This very manifestation, suffused with the sequence of various objects and abiding within, pervading the sequence of all moments of awareness (<s>saṃvit</s>), consisting of infinite consciousness (<s>Cit</s>), designated as the Self, is the knowing subject (<s>pramātṛ</s>); and [He is] <s>Maheśvara</s> (the Great Lord) by virtue of being the creator (<s>nirmātṛ</s>) with respect to the knowable (<s>prameya</s>) which is His own limb.
Through the various mouths of differentiated awareness (<s>saṃvitti</s>),
in the single knowing subject (<s>ekapramātṛ</s>),
when entities come to rest,
this cognition (<s>jñātā</s>) is established.

children.text: Ipv: anekasaṃvitsrotomukhair ekapramātṛsindhum upalīya bhāvabhedāḥ kāryakāraṇatādivyavahārasamanvayaṃ bhajante //
children.translated_text: Ipv: Through the many streams and mouths of awareness (<s>saṃvit</s>), the differentiated entities, merging into the single ocean of the knowing subject (<s>pramātṛ</s>), partake of the connection of practical activity such as cause and effect and so forth.
Of those that partake of the sequence of space, time,
of things that are self-contained,
that [unity] is accomplished by a single manifestation (<s>ābhāsa</s>);
otherwise, what connection (<s>samanvaya</s>) could there be?

children.text: Ipv: svarūpam avabhāsanaṃ ca bhāvānāṃ svātmapariniṣṭhitam eva / yugapadekābhāsanibandhanaś caiṣāṃ samanvayaḥ / sa abhinnaḥ pramātṛlīnatayā kalpate /
children.translated_text: Ipv: The own nature and manifestation of entities is established in their own self alone. And the connection (<s>samanvaya</s>) of these is grounded in a simultaneous single manifestation (<s>ābhāsa</s>). That [connection], being undifferentiated, is possible only through subsidence in the cognizer (<s>pramātṛ</s>).
Of perceptions and non-apprehensions
which fall upon respectively distinct aspects,
the establishment of cause-and-effect relation
has as its ground the single cognizer (<s>pramātṛ</s>).

children.text: Ipv: kāryakāraṇabhāva iva tatsiddhir api pratyakṣānupalambhair ekapramātṛmukhena samanvayam āgatya kriyate, asamanvitāḥ pratyakṣānupalambhāḥ kramikasvaviṣayamātrajñāpanakṣīṇā nānyonyāpekṣopalakṣaṇakṣamāḥ //
children.translated_text: Ipv: Just as the cause-and-effect relation itself, so too its establishment is accomplished through perceptions and non-apprehensions arriving at connection (<s>samanvaya</s>) by means of a single cognizer (<s>pramātṛ</s>). Perceptions and non-apprehensions that have not arrived at connection, being exhausted in merely making known their own respective successive objects, are incapable of mutually determining one another.
The very self-awareness (<s>svasaṃvitti</s>) in memory
that is the means of valid knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>) for its own occurrence,
is also the sole means of establishing
the existence of the prior experience, and nothing else.

children.text: Ipv: pūrvānubhasvasaṃvedanasya abhāvāt smṛtisvasaṃvedanam eva atraikārthābhāsamayapramātṛrūpaṃ smṛtisvarūpa iva pramāṇam / smṛteḥ pūrvānubhavābhāsābhāve kāryakāraṇabhāvāsiddher na kāryaliṅgatā //
children.translated_text: Ipv: Since there is no self-awareness (<s>svasaṃvedana</s>) of the prior experience [as such], the self-awareness of memory alone, having the form of the cognizer (<s>pramātṛ</s>) in whom a single object appears, is the means of valid knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>) just as it is for the nature of memory itself. In the absence of the appearance of the prior experience within the cognition of memory, since the cause-and-effect relation would not be established, there is no inferability from an effect.
The relation of sublator and sublated (<s>bādhyabādhakabhāva</s>) too
would arise among cognitions that are non-contradictory
in their own self-established [natures] only through
establishment in a single cognizer (<s>pramātṛ</s>).

children.text: Ipv: bhinnasvābhāsamātraniṣṭhānāṃ jñānānāṃ ko virodhaḥ, tat kathaṃ bādhyabādhkatvam / ekaprāmātṛviśrāntau tu yuktam //
children.translated_text: Ipv: What contradiction could there be among cognitions that are established merely in their own distinct appearances (<s>ābhāsa</s>)? How then could there be sublation (<s>bādhyabādhaktva</s>)? But it is appropriate when they rest in a single cognizer (<s>pramātṛ</s>).
Just as the cognition of a bare ground
is the awareness of the absence of a pot,
so too, if the cognition of mother-of-pearl
were the knower of the invalidity of the cognition of silver—

children.text: Ipv: iha bhūtale ghaṭo nāstīti ghaṭābhāvajñānaṃ kevalabhūtalajñānam eva śūnyabhūtalasya ghaṭābhāvarūpatvāt / tathaiva yadi śuktikārajatayor aparasparātmatvāc chuktikājñānaṃ rajatājñānam iti pratyakṣaṃ bādhakam //
children.translated_text: Ipv: Here, the cognition 'there is no pot on this ground' is merely the cognition of the bare ground, since the empty ground has the nature of the absence of a pot. In the same way, if—because mother-of-pearl and silver are not each other's nature—the cognition of mother-of-pearl were [identical with] the non-cognition of silver, then perception would be the sublator (<s>bādhaka</s>).
But it is not so: from the cognition of the bare ground
only its non-pot nature is established,
but not the absence of the pot-nature
of that which is fit to be perceived here.

children.text: Ipv: kevalabhūtalajnānād bhūtalasyāghaṭātmatā sidhyati, na tu tatrādhāre bhinno darśanayogyo 'pi ghaṭo nāsti //
children.translated_text: Ipv: From the cognition of the bare ground alone, the non-pot nature of the ground is established, but not that a pot which is distinct and fit to be seen is absent there on that substrate.
The ground is always bare [of other things]
due to the self-established nature of entities;
so how could the cognition of it ever
be a means of establishing the absence of something distinct?

children.text: Ipv: bhūtalam abhūtalaviviktaṃ sadaiva tat kathaṃ tajjñānaṃ kadācid eva tatra bhinnaghaṭābhāvaṃ sādhayet / bhinnaghaṭaviviktatā ca bhūtalasya kadācit kaṃ rūpaṃ syād yadi ghaṭasahitatāpi kadācit svarūpaṃ bhavet, na tv evam / padārtau dvav eva svātmapariniṣṭhitau, sāhityaṃ na tadatiriktam ubhayātmakam ekarūpam / jñānam ekaṃ tūbhayābhāsasaṃsargātmakam apy ekābhāsajñānāntarābhāvarūpam / vastu punaḥ svātmaniṣṭham eva paricchinattīti na vastubalena pradeśadarśanāt pradeśasiddhivad ghaṭābhāvasiddhiḥ / ubhayābhāsaikajñānātmakakāryābhāvāt tu syāt / na caivaṃ vyavadhānena pratītiḥ pradeśadarśanād eva tatsiddheḥ //
children.translated_text: Ipv: The ground is always distinct from what is not the ground; so how could its cognition establish the absence of a distinct pot only sometimes? And the distinctness of the ground from a pot—what form would that take at some particular time, if its being accompanied by a pot were also at some time its own nature? But this is not so. The two entities are simply self-established in themselves; their togetherness is not something additional to them having a single nature comprising both. However, a single cognition, though having the nature of a conjunction of two appearances (<s>ābhāsa</s>), has the form of the absence of another appearance within one appearance. But a real entity cognizes only what is established in itself, so the establishment of the absence of a pot does not follow from seeing a location merely by the force of the object, as the establishment of a location follows from seeing a location. Rather, it would follow from the absence of the effect that consists in a single cognition of both appearances. But perception does not occur thus through an intermediary, since the establishment [of the location] comes from seeing the location itself.
But suppose a mass of light, or for a blind person
a soft touch such as warmth and the like—
existing there—were to establish through its own cognition
the non-pot nature [of that place].

children.text: Ipv: pradeśeṣv ālokapuraṃ santamase mṛdum uṣṇādikaṃ sparśaṃ vā ghaṭarūpasparśābhāvātmakam anubhūyālokādi ghaṭābhāvo 'trāsti, ghaṭo nāstīti vyavahartuṃ yuktam //
children.translated_text: Ipv: Having experienced in certain locations a mass of light in complete darkness, or a soft touch such as warmth—which has the nature of the absence of the form and touch of a pot—it is appropriate to engage in the conventional usage 'the absence of a pot exists here, the pot does not exist.'
A demon (<s>piśāca</s>) may be invisible even
within the range of light, just as—
being invisible within the ground—
it cannot be negated in every way.

children.text: Ipv: na caivam ālokasya piśācānyatvāt tatra piśācaniṣedhaprasaṅgaḥ, sa hy adṛśyo 'nyatve 'pi yathā mṛdgolakasyāpy antaranivāryas tathālokasyāntare / tatas tasya anyamata ivāsmanmate 'pi nādṛśyatvād abhāvasiddhiḥ //
children.translated_text: Ipv: Nor in this way is there the unwanted consequence of negating a demon (<s>piśāca</s>) within the light, since the light is different from the demon; for the demon, being invisible, even though different [from the ground], cannot be excluded from within a clay ball, just as it cannot from within the light. Therefore, in our view as in the opponent's view, the establishment of absence does not follow from invisibility.
Thus the cognition of mother-of-pearl would have the form
of the absence of the cognition of silver,
but it would not be the knower of the invalidity
of the initial cognition of silver.

children.text: Ipv: śuktijñānam eva rajatajñānābhāvarūpaṃ sidhyati, tadānīntanaśuktijñānānubhavena na bhinnasyātītasya rūpyajñānasyāprāmāṇyam //
children.translated_text: Ipv: Only the cognition of mother-of-pearl having the form of the absence of the cognition of silver is established; the invalidity of the distinct, past cognition of silver is not [established] by the present experience of the cognition of mother-of-pearl.
Even from inference there could be no sublation (<s>bādhā</s>)
when the property-bearer (<s>dharmin</s>) is not established;
but [sublation] grounded in self-awareness (<s>svasaṃvedana</s>)
is appropriate, being born of a single cognizer (<s>pramātṛ</s>).

children.text: Ipv: śuktikājñānakāle ca na pūrvaṃ rajatajñānam asti / tataḥ sa dharmī na siddha iti nānumānena bādhā, ekapramātṛmayasvasaṃvedane tv ekadeśāvaṣṭambhyubhayajñānamayasaṃbandhabhāsanāt sidhyati / paścātsaṃvādaḥ pratyakṣasvasaṃvedane pūrvasyāpi tasya bhāsanād ekaṃ pramāṇam itarad anyatheti bhavati / saṃvādo 'py ekapramātṛkṛtaḥ //
children.translated_text: Ipv: At the time of the cognition of mother-of-pearl, the prior cognition of silver does not exist. Therefore, since that property-bearer (<s>dharmin</s>) is not established, there is no sublation through inference. But in self-awareness (<s>svasaṃvedana</s>) pervaded by a single cognizer (<s>pramātṛ</s>), [sublation] is established because the relation constituted by both cognitions shines forth, with one part as the basis. The subsequent corroboration (<s>saṃvāda</s>), since in direct self-awareness (<s>svasaṃvedana</s>) the former [cognition] too appears, becomes: 'one is a valid means of knowledge, the other is otherwise.' Corroboration too is accomplished by a single cognizer.
In this way, in the all-pervading one (<s>vibhu</s>)
who is studded with appearances (<s>ābhāsa</s>) of extremely diverse objects,
conventional activity is experienced
as either impure or pure.

children.text: Ipv: māyāśaktyā bhedaviṣayo 'yaṃ sarvo vyavahāras tathājñānaināṃ śuddho 'jñānāndhānāṃ tu malinas tattadbhinnārthāvabhāsabhāji bhagavati saṃbhāvyate 'nubhavena //
children.translated_text: Ipv: Through the power of <s>māyā</s>, all this conventional activity whose object is difference is thus attributed to the Lord (<s>bhagavat</s>) who partakes of the appearances of respectively distinct objects—pure for those with knowledge, impure for those blinded by ignorance—as experienced.
Thus ends the seventh chapter (<s>āhnika</s>) of the Section on Knowledge (<s>Jñānādhikāra</s>).
Appearances (<s>ābhāsa</s>) are, in some cases, dependent
on the presence of sense faculties at that time,
but in other cases, such as for the blind
and in total darkness, they are otherwise.

children.text: Ipv: ābhāsāḥ kadācit sannihitapratyakṣākṣiptā ghaṭo 'yam iti vyavahārahetavaḥ, andhatamasādau tu pūrvānubhavotthitāḥ //
children.translated_text: Ipv: Appearances (<s>ābhāsa</s>) are sometimes caused by proximate perception, being the grounds for conventional usage such as 'this is a pot'; but in the case of the blind, in darkness, and so forth, they arise from prior experience.
There is no distinction of the appearance of an object
with respect to [its] existence (<s>sattā</s>) anywhere;
it may exist in <s>vikalpas</s> (conceptual cognitions)
that pertain to future, present, and past objects.

children.text: Ipv: smṛtyutprekṣārūpeṣu pratyakṣapṛṣṭhapātiṣu svatantreṣu vānyeṣu vikalpeṣu kālatrayaviṣayeṣv arthāvabhāso 'ntas tulya evāvasthitaḥ //
children.translated_text: Ipv: In <s>vikalpas</s> (conceptual cognitions) of the form of memory, imagination, and the like—whether following upon direct perception or independent—pertaining to objects of all three times, the internal appearance of an object remains the same throughout.
In the case of pleasure and so forth, and of pleasantness and the like,
and even in the case of causal objects,
though the appearance has existence,
it remains so [inert] due to being past.

children.text: Ipv: sukhaduḥkhādyābhāsās tatsādhanābhāsāś ca sadaivāntaḥ santo 'pi na tadāhlādādimayīṃ sthitiṃ kurvanty atītatvād bahis tadānīm abhāvāt tadātvaviśiṣṭānāṃ ca tathākāritvāt //
children.translated_text: Ipv: The appearances (<s>ābhāsa</s>) of pleasure, pain, and the like, as well as the appearances of their means, though always existing internally, do not produce a state of delight and so forth because they are past—being absent externally at that time—and because those qualified by temporal presentness alone are of that effective nature.
But when pleasure and the like are vividly
traced by a <s>vikalpa</s> (conceptual cognition),
such a state occurs just so,
clearly, due to its distinct apprehension.

children.text: Ipv: kutaś cit prayatnaniveśāt svatantravikalpollikhitaṃ sphuṭam eva sukhādi jātaṃ vikāsādihetuḥ //
children.translated_text: Ipv: Due to a certain effort of immersion, pleasure and the like, vividly traced by an independent <s>vikalpa</s>, arise clearly and become the cause of blossoming [of experience] and so forth.
Externality is considered to be a limiting condition (<s>upādhi</s>)
of appearances of existence and non-existence,
not their essence; therefore their existence (<s>sattā</s>)
is always that of internal [realities] that exist.

children.text: Ipv: sarveṣām ābhāsānāṃ bhāvābhāvaviṣayānām abahīrūpatve 'pi sattāsty eva smṛtyādau, bāhyatvam hi teṣām upādhir na svarūpam / abhāvābhāsasyāntaḥsattāyām api bahirabhāvāt tathātvam //
children.translated_text: Ipv: Of all appearances (<s>ābhāsa</s>), whether pertaining to existence or non-existence, even when they lack external form, existence persists as in memory and the like; for externality is a limiting condition (<s>upādhi</s>) of them, not their own nature. Even when the appearance of absence has internal existence, its status as such [i.e., as absence] is due to its external non-existence.
Due to being internal, in the unity of the cognizer (<s>pramātṛ</s>),
there is no purposeful activity (<s>arthakriyā</s>) of these
grounded in difference; but in the case of externality,
that [activity] varies according to the difference of distinct appearances.

children.text: Ipv: antaś ca sarveṣām eva nīlasukhādyā bhāsānām sadā sattve 'pi pramātṛmātrarūpatvāt kāryakāraṇādibhedāśrayā nārthakriyā, pramātur bhede 'pi bauddhacākṣuṣatvādibhedenābhāsabhedād ābhāsāśritārthakāritāpi bhidyate rūpādīnām //
children.translated_text: Ipv: Internally, even though all appearances such as blue, pleasure, and so forth always have existence, there is no purposeful activity (<s>arthakriyā</s>) grounded in distinctions such as cause and effect, since they have merely the form of the cognizer (<s>pramātṛ</s>). Even when the cognizer is differentiated—by distinctions such as intellectual, visual, and so forth—the purposeful activity dependent on appearances also becomes differentiated due to the difference of appearances, as in the case of forms and the like.
Since appearances are of the nature of consciousness (<s>cit</s>),
their abiding is always internal;
but for those that appear through <s>māyā</s>,
that [abiding] is also external, due to [their] externality.

children.text: Ipv: citsvarūpatvenābhāsānāṃ sadāntastattva eva sthitiḥ / māyāśaktyā bahiḥ pratyakṣatvena prakāśyamāneṣu bhāveṣu prakāśāvyatirikteṣu bahirābhāsa ity ucyate, tad api teṣām āntaratvam eva sisṛkṣādau tu bhāvānām api //
children.translated_text: Ipv: Due to having the nature of consciousness (<s>cit</s>), the abiding of appearances is always in the internal reality. When entities are made manifest externally through the power of <s>māyā</s> in the form of direct perception—entities that are not different from <s>prakāśa</s> (consciousness-light)—this is called 'external appearance,' yet even that is really their internality. But at the stage of the desire to create (<s>sisṛkṣā</s>), [this applies] even to entities.
The tracing (<s>ullekha</s>) that occurs in <s>vikalpa</s>
is also external, being a separate manifestation;
internality is identity with the cognizer (<s>pramātṛ</s>),
while difference from that is externality.

children.text: Ipv: vikalpe ghaṭādyullekhaś cakṣurādyagocare 'pi pṛthagābhāsād bāhya eva / ahaṃvimarśo hy āntaratvaṃ, idam iti tu bāhyatā / evaṃ ca ghaṭādīnām ubhayī bāhyatā bāhyāntaḥkaraṇadvayīvedyatā, sukhādes tv ekāntaḥkaraṇavedyataiva //
children.translated_text: Ipv: The tracing (<s>ullekha</s>) of a pot and the like in <s>vikalpa</s>, even when not within the range of the eye and other senses, is external precisely because of its separate appearance (<s>ābhāsa</s>). For the 'I'-reflective awareness (<s>ahaṃvimarśa</s>) is internality, while 'this' is externality. Thus, for pots and the like there is a twofold externality—being known by both the external and internal instruments; but for pleasure and the like, there is only the single internality of being known by the internal instrument alone.
The illumination (<s>prakāśa</s>) of the tracing (<s>ullekha</s>)
and of pleasure and the like is externally, by the Self,
in the form of direct experience (<s>adhyakṣa</s>), by the will of the Lord (<s>bhartṛ</s>),
just as that of things born of the senses and the like.

children.text: Ipv: ullekhasukhaduḥkhalajjādīnāṃ cākṣuṣānāṃ rūpādīnām iveśvarasya śaktyā sākṣātkaraṇarūpo bauddhaḥ prakāśaḥ //
children.translated_text: Ipv: The intellectual illumination (<s>prakāśa</s>) of tracings (<s>ullekha</s>), of pleasure, pain, shame, and the like, takes the form of direct apprehension (<s>sākṣātkaraṇa</s>) through the power of <s>Īśvara</s> (the Lord), just like the [illumination] of visual forms and the like.
Without unity with that [cognizer],
the course of worldly experience (<s>lokapaddhati</s>) of cognitions would not exist;
that unity is due to the unity of <s>prakāśa</s> (consciousness-light);
it is established that that single one is the cognizer (<s>mātṛ</s>).

children.text: Ipv: tattadvibhinnasaṃvidanusandhānena hi vyavahāraḥ / ekaś ca prakāśātmā tadanusandhānarūpaḥ sa eva caikaḥ pramātā paramātmasaṃjñaḥ //
children.translated_text: Ipv: For it is through the synthetic unity (<s>anusandhāna</s>) of respectively distinct cognitions that conventional activity operates. And the one who is of the nature of <s>prakāśa</s> (consciousness-light), whose form is that very synthetic unity—he alone is the single cognizer (<s>pramātṛ</s>), called <s>Paramātman</s> (the Supreme Self).
He, by virtue of his definite nature
as the reflectively aware one, is <s>Maheśvara</s> (the Great Lord);
for the pure knowledge and action of the deity
are nothing but <s>vimarśa</s> (reflective awareness).

children.text: Ipv: sa paramātmā cidrūpovimarśākhyenaiva mukhyasvabhāvenāvyabicāriṇā maheśvaraḥ / cittattvasya viśvātmanaḥ śivasaṃjñasyāhaṃvimarśanam eva śuddhe jñānakriye, bhinnābhinnajñeyakāryagate tv īśvarasya śuddhāśuddhe, bhinnārthaviṣaye tu puṃsaḥ sattvarajovṛttirūpe prakāśapravṛttisaṃjñe tamasā saṃkucite 'śuddhe eva//
children.translated_text: Ipv: That <s>Paramātman</s> (Supreme Self), by his principal, invariable nature called <s>vimarśa</s> (reflective awareness), whose essence is consciousness (<s>cit</s>), is <s>Maheśvara</s>. The 'I'-reflective awareness (<s>ahaṃvimarśana</s>) of the <s>cit-tattva</s> (consciousness-principle), which has the universe as its nature and bears the name <s>Śiva</s>, constitutes pure knowledge and action. But when directed toward objects that are both distinct and non-distinct from the known and the effected, they are the pure-impure [knowledge and action] of <s>Īśvara</s>. When directed toward distinct objects, they are [the faculties] of the individual soul (<s>puṃs</s>) in the form of <s>sattva</s> and <s>rajas</s> functions—called illumination (<s>prakāśa</s>) and activity (<s>pravṛtti</s>)—contracted by <s>tamas</s>, and are impure alone.
Thus ends the eighth chapter (<s>āhnika</s>) of the Section on Knowledge (<s>Jñānādhikāra</s>).
Thus ends the Section on Knowledge (<s>Jñānādhikāra</s>).
The Section on Action (<s>Kriyādhikāra</s>).
First chapter (<s>āhnika</s>).
Therefore, what was also stated—
that sequential action (<s>kriyā</s>) is not possible for a single [entity]—
that, beginning with 'of a single one,' has been refuted
through the demonstration of the single [consciousness-principle].

children.text: Ipv: ekacittattvasamarthanād ekasaṃbandhī vyāpāra eka eveti kriyāpy apakṛtadūṣaṇā //
children.translated_text: Ipv: Through the demonstration of the single <s>cit-tattva</s> (consciousness-principle), the activity related to a single [entity] is one alone; thus action (<s>kriyā</s>) too has its objection removed.
The sequential nature (<s>sakramatva</s>) of worldly
action (<s>kriyā</s>) is possible due to the power of time (<s>kālaśakti</s>),
but not [the sequential nature] of the eternal [action]
that is the innate nature of the Lord (<s>prabhu</s>).

children.text: Ipv: māyāśakter bhinnabhāvāvabhāsānāṃ kriyā ca kālaśaktivaśāt sakramā na tv ātmavimarśarūpānādinidhanā prabhoḥ svabhāvabhūtā //
children.translated_text: Ipv: The action (<s>kriyā</s>) of the appearances of distinct entities [produced] by the power of <s>māyā</s> is sequential due to the power of time (<s>kālaśakti</s>); but the [action] that is the innate nature (<s>svabhāvabhūtā</s>) of the Lord, having the form of self-reflective awareness (<s>ātmavimarśa</s>), beginningless and endless, is not [sequential].
Time (<s>kāla</s>) is the movement of the sun and the like,
or the birth of particular flowers and so forth,
or heat and cold—but what is indicated by these
is in truth nothing but sequence (<s>krama</s>).

children.text: Ipv: sā sā prasiddhā kriyā kālaḥ śītādi vā tadupalakṣitaḥ sarvabhinnāvabhāsamānabhāvopādhibhūtaḥ krama eva vāsau tasyaivopayogāt //
children.translated_text: Ipv: Each well-known action—time, or heat and cold, or what is indicated by them—is in essence nothing but sequence (<s>krama</s>), which serves as the limiting condition (<s>upādhi</s>) of all the distinct entities that appear, since it is sequence alone that is of use [in these cases].
Sequence (<s>krama</s>) depends on difference; difference too
depends on the existence and non-existence of appearances (<s>ābhāsa</s>);
the existence and non-existence of appearances, however,
is brought about by the variegated manifestation of the Lord (<s>prabhu</s>).
Ipv: The variegated creative activity of the Lord, consisting in the appearance of distinct entities that are devoid of each other's appearance, is itself the cause of sequence in entities.
He manifests spatial sequence
through the variety of forms,
and temporal sequence through the manifestation
of the variety of actions—[this is] <s>Īśvara</s> (the Lord).

children.text: Ipv: anekasyānyonyabhedābhāsād deśakramaḥ kriyāmukhena kālakramo 'pi / ekasya tu bhāvasya tattajjanmasattāvipariṇāmādikriyābhedāt kālakrama eva //
children.translated_text: Ipv: Spatial sequence arises from the mutual difference of appearance of many [entities]; temporal sequence also [arises] by means of action. For a single entity, however, there is only temporal sequence, due to the differentiation of actions such as birth, existence, transformation, and the like.
Everywhere, even the difference of appearances
would be the repository of temporal sequence,
for the cognizer (<s>mātṛ</s>) whose appearance is interrupted—[as in the case of]
the void and the like—not for what has appeared all at once.

children.text: Ipv: sarvatrārthe vicitro 'vabhāsaḥ śūnyadehāder eva pramātuḥ kālakramābhāsahetur, sa hi prākkālo na tathā tadānīṃ bhāsate smṛtiṃ vihāya svavartamānāpekṣayā cāsau bhūtabhaviṣyatte vyavaharati / sakṛdvibhātasya tu bhāsanakriyāvicchedād āvṛttigaṇanābhāvān nātmanīvārtheṣv api kālabhedaḥ /
children.translated_text: Ipv: In every object, the variegated appearance (<s>avabhāsa</s>)—being of the cognizer (<s>pramātṛ</s>) alone, [arising] from the void, body, and the like—is the cause of the appearance of temporal sequence. For the previous time does not appear the same way at that [later] moment, setting aside memory; and it is in relation to one's own present that one engages in the conventional usage of past and future. But for what has shone forth all at once, since there is no interruption of the activity of appearing and hence no counting of repetitions, there is no temporal differentiation in objects as there is in the self.
Spatial sequence in entities also
appears for the cognizer (<s>mātṛ</s>) of limited nature;
but for the unlimited one, entities shine forth
as full in themselves, by themselves.

children.text: Ipv: parimitaṃ pramātaram apekṣya bhāvas tato 'nyonyaṃ ca bhinnā dūrādivyapadeśabhājaś ca, prakāśaikarūpatvena tv īśvarasya na kvāpy \var{kvāpy\lem \em kvapy \ed} aprakāśasaṃbhavāt paramāṇav api / prakāśaghanasya nātmano bhinnaṃ dūraṃ vānyānyato vā kiṃcid ābhāti //
children.translated_text: Ipv: In relation to a limited cognizer (<s>pramātṛ</s>), entities are distinct from one another and from him, and are subject to designations such as 'far' and the like. But for <s>Īśvara</s> (the Lord), due to having the single form of <s>prakāśa</s> (consciousness-light), there is nowhere the possibility of non-illumination, even in atoms. For the one who is a mass of <s>prakāśa</s>, nothing appears as distinct, distant, or separate from the Self in any way.
But that very power of creation (<s>nirmāṇaśakti</s>)
belongs to the one who knows thus and who is the Lord (<s>īśitṛ</s>);
[it is the reason] that the distinction of knower (<s>vijñātṛ</s>)
and known (<s>vijñeya</s>) is manifested.

children.text: Ipv: evaṃ pūrṇatayā prakāśamānasyāpi parameśvarasya saiṣā sṛṣṭiśaktir yaj jñātṛjñeyasvabhāvā bhāvāḥ svato 'nyonyaṃ ca vibhāgenāvasīyante, na ca tathāvasāyena tasya svarūpasthitis tirodhīyate //
children.translated_text: Ipv: Even though the Supreme Lord (<s>Parameśvara</s>) appears as full [in this way], this creative power (<s>sṛṣṭiśakti</s>) of his is the reason that entities, whose nature is that of knower and known, are determined as distinct from themselves and from one another; yet by such determination his abiding in his own nature is not concealed.
Thus ends the first chapter (<s>āhnika</s>) of the Section on Action (<s>Kriyādhikāra</s>).
Second chapter (<s>āhnika</s>).
The cognitions of action (<s>kriyā</s>), relation (<s>saṃbandha</s>), universal (<s>sāmānya</s>),
substance (<s>dravya</s>), space (<s>dik</s>), time (<s>kāla</s>), and intellect (<s>buddhi</s>)
are considered real, due to [their] stability and utility,
and as having both singular and plural substrata.

children.text: Ipv: kriyāvad anye 'pi saṃbandhādaya ekānekaviṣayā api satyābhāsāḥ, sarvadopayoginām eṣām arthavattvenāpariharaṇīyatvāt //
children.translated_text: Ipv: Like action (<s>kriyā</s>), the other [categories] too—relation and so forth—even though pertaining to both singular and plural objects, are appearances of reality, since these, being always useful, cannot be set aside due to their meaningfulness.
There, the one internal reality,
that very [reality], attaining the state of being cognized by the senses,
becomes manifold
by virtue of place, time, and intrinsic nature.

children.text: Ipv: abhinnam eva tattvam anto bahir ābhāsabhedād ekānekam, bahirdeśakālasvabhāvabhedābhāsasaṃbhedamayaikaikaḥ svalakṣaṇābhāsānām anekatvāt //
children.translated_text: Ipv: The undifferentiated reality itself, internally and externally, through the difference of <s>ābhāsas</s> (manifestations), is one and many—each external [manifestation] being a composite of manifestations of differences in place, time, and intrinsic nature, [and] manifold due to the multiplicity of <s>svalakṣaṇa</s>-manifestations (particular-appearances). //
These [cognitions], having both [internal and external] as their objects—
the mind, the subsequent determiner, being real,
produces conceptions of action and the like
that are of the nature of the knower's activity.

Ipv: Standing in the middle, the mental [cognitions] pertaining to both internal and external reality are conceptions of action and the like, which are of the nature of the <s>pramātṛ</s>'s (knower's) activity. //
Entities abiding in one's own Self, having distinct appearances,
in a single <s>pramātṛ</s> (knower),
possessing the unity of mutual connection—
[these are] the ground for the cognition of relation.

children.text: Ipv: rājñaḥ puruṣa ityādisaṃbandhadhiyo 'ntaḥsamanvayād aikyaṃ bahiḥ saṃbandhibhedaṃ cālambante //
